name: Basil
variety: Species-level sweet-basil crop identity; cultivar unspecified
summary: A species-level basil profile for records labeled only “Basil.” It is distinct from Genovese, Sweet Basil, and named basil types; cultivar-specific traits are not inferred.

identity.short: Species identity: Ocimum basilicum; cultivar unspecified
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Ocimum basilicum. This profile represents basil where no cultivar or horticultural type is identified. Genovese, Sweet, Thai, and other named types remain separate identities.

cultivation.short: Warm-season herb for a sunny, well-drained site
cultivation.guidance: USU Extension recommends full sun, warm conditions, regular moisture, and well-drained soil for basil generally. This crop-level guidance is not a claim about any one named cultivar and does not establish hydroponic nutrient suitability.

growth.short: Annual herb or subshrub, with form varying across cultivars
growth.guidance: Kew describes O. basilicum as an annual or subshrub and notes variation among cultivars. No single mature height or growth form is assigned to this cultivar-unspecified profile.

harvest.short: USU begins harvest after plants develop 6–8 leaves
harvest.guidance: USU Extension gives 6–8 leaves as a harvest-readiness cue for basil and advises cutting stems while retaining several leaves. The timing is general basil guidance, not a cultivar-specific harvest date.

maintenance.short: Regular leaf harvest before flowering supports continued foliage
maintenance.guidance: USU Extension says regular leaf removal before flowers form encourages more leaves and branches. Its FAQ cautions that pinching flowers alone does not stimulate new foliage and may encourage flowers in leaf axils. This is general O. basilicum guidance, not a cultivar-specific pruning schedule.

problems.short: Heat and water stress can promote flowering; watch for rot and leaf injury
problems.guidance: USU Extension notes that high summer temperature and water stress can promote flowering and that root rot and basil shoot blight may occur. These are crop-level observations; no cultivar-specific resistance is claimed.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: General garden basil guidance does not establish hydroponic nutrient requirements or performance for this identity.

growthHabits.reason: Kew notes that growth form varies by cultivar; none is identified here.

height.reason: Cultivar-unspecified basil varies in mature size.

spread.reason: Cultivar-unspecified basil varies in mature spread.

spacing.reason: Outdoor crop spacing is not a hydroponic pod-spacing recommendation.

evidence.note: USU recommends full sun for basil in garden culture; this outdoor exposure is not translated into an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Bunching Onion
summary: Allium fistulosum is a non-bulbing scallion grown for green and white stalks. Keep it distinct from immature bulb onions and Egyptian walking onion; the cited water and weed guidance is regional outdoor Extension advice.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Allium fistulosum. UMN Extension identifies scallions/bunching onions as A. fistulosum and distinguishes Egyptian walking onion (A. cepa var. proliferum). This entry has no named cultivar and does not replace Nebuka or White Lisbon.

cultivation.short: Full sun; keep soil evenly watered and seedlings weeded
cultivation.guidance: UMN recommends a sunny location, watering when rainfall is insufficient, and frequent gentle weed control while plants are small. These are outdoor garden recommendations, not hydroponic system specifications.

growth.short: Green and white stalks without a formed bulb
growth.guidance: UMN describes A. fistulosum scallions as green and white stalks that do not form bulbs. This species-level description is not a claim about all green onions, which may also be immature A. cepa.

care.short: Keep the shallow-rooted crop evenly moist and weeded
care.guidance: UMN Extension notes that scallions are shallow-rooted, need steady moisture, and are easily outcompeted by weeds while small. Weed gently and frequently; the page's weekly rainfall target is Minnesota outdoor guidance, not a universal indoor or hydroponic instruction.

problems.short: Yellowing and wilting need diagnosis, not an automatic disease label
problems.guidance: UMN lists onion maggot as one cause of yellowing and wilting in scallions and also notes several possible rots. These are crop-group possibilities, not a diagnosis of this identity; inspect roots and stalks and seek local diagnostic help before treatment.

harvest.short: Pull scallions when they reach usable size
harvest.guidance: UMN advises pulling scallions when they reach usable size and loosening soil first if needed to avoid breaking stalks. No fixed days-to-harvest is assigned to this cultivar-unspecified identity.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Garden scallion guidance does not establish long-term hydroponic performance.

evidence.note: UMN documents the non-bulbing species form; clumping is supported by the general A. fistulosum crop identity but not a specific cultivar.

height.reason: No cultivar-independent mature height is selected for this profile.

spread.reason: No cultivar-independent mature spread is selected for this profile.

spacing.reason: Outdoor spacing is not a hydroponic pod-spacing recommendation.

evidence.note: UMN says onions require full sun for best garden growth; this is outdoor exposure, not an indoor lamp tier.
